newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia stocks mixed, fund selling saps Dow's impact.
newsitem.headline: Asia stocks mixed, fund selling saps Dow's impact.

text.p: Asia stock markets ended mixed on Monday as selling by fund managers in several markets sapped the impact of Wall Street's powerful rally on Friday, which followed news of weaker-than-expected U.S. jobs figures.
Thai stocks in particular were hard hit, with the key index falling more than six percent as Friday's news of stricter bank lending regulations led to heavy selling of bank and finance stocks.
Hong Kong stocks staged the most impressive rally, with the Hang Seng index scoring its biggest point gain since March. It closed 227.56 points, or 1.91 percent, higher at 12,133.07.

"Investors are really encouraged by what we saw in the States and the possibility that interest rates will not have to be raised so quickly," said Kent Rossiter, institutional sales manager at Nikko Securities.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 60 points on Friday to close 1.01 percent higher at 5,993. The U.S. Treasury's key 30-year bond soared 1-1/4 points, pushing the yield down to 6.74 percent, the lowest in two months.

The catalyst for the gains was an unexpected drop of 40,000 in the September non-farm payrolls figure reported on Friday, which was contrary to the 166,000 gain economists had forecast and a rise of 241,000 in August.
Bond traders viewed the news as a sign the U.S. economy was slowing and that the Federal Reserve acted appropriately when it decided to leave interest rates unchanged at its recent meeting.
Tokyo blue chips reversed an early downturn to end slightly higher, with the key Nikkei 225-share index up 12.98 points, or 0.06 percent, at 21,161.01. Other market indicators were lower.
Early weakness was attributed to anxiety over the long-awaited listing of West Japan Railway Co on Tuesday and uncertainty about the outcome of the upcoming general election.

Seoul stocks zoomed ahead to end 18.02 points, or 2.32 percent, higher at 795.33 on broad-based buying and expectations of lower interest rates following an economic ministers meeting on Wednesday, which will be headed by President Kim Young-sam.
Australia's All Ordinaries Index was up 24.3 points, or 1.05 percent, at 2,339.8, while New Zealand shares closed 30.48 points, or 1.36 percent, higher at 2,274.76.

Elsewhere in Asia, Malaysian and Indonesian shares erased early gains and turned lower on profit-taking. Malaysia's key index was off 1.68 points, or 0.15 percent, at 1,148.50, while Indonesian shares fell 2.038, or 0.35 percent, to 586.311.
Philippine shares ended lower, although off the lows, with the key index down 10.11 points, or 0.32 percent, at 3,121.03.
Property stocks were hit hard, particularly Ayala Land, on expectations that the real estate boom may be fizzling and heavy selling by a major foreign fund, one broker said.

In Bangkok, traders noted that the concern over new bank lending restrictions only further dampened sentiment, which has been steadily eroded by expectations of a weak economy and a steady monetary policy.

Taiwan shares turned lower on concern over the growing tensions between Tokyo and Taipei in a dispute over the Diaoyu (Senkaku) Islands. The weighted index closed down 24.24 points, or 0.36 percent, at 6,620.42.

Singapore's Straits Times Index also fell, reflecting a slowdown in key industry sectors and uncertainty over the island-state's general election, which must be held by April next year. The index ended down 22.20 points, or 1.03 percent, at 2,126.66.
At 1027 GMT, the dollar was at 111.48/1.53 yen and 1.5305/10 marks.
Bullion ended at US$379.50/380.00, against New York's US$380.25/75 close.
SIMEX North Sea Brent crude oil futures for November were slightly lower at $23.80 a barrel, down five cents from London's settlement on Friday at $23.85.
